readings.title: An apprentice learns by explaining
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A bicycle workshop welcomed two adult apprentices. Both could repeat repair steps, but their supervisor wanted to know whether they understood the reasons behind them. The central difficulty was memorised steps without clear understanding. The apprentices followed a printed list carefully yet could not explain why a damaged part needed replacing before another adjustment. The organizers knew that a tidy plan in an office might not match what happened in an ordinary week.

The group first tried brief explanations during each repair. After completing a safe task, each learner described the purpose of the step to a partner and asked one question about the method. They therefore listened to people who used the place at different times, including those who seldom attended formal meetings.

The trial showed questions exposed gaps before mistakes became habits. A conversation about brake cables revealed confusion that a completed checklist would not have shown to the supervisor. In response, the group adopted a shared explanation notebook. The team wrote short notes in plain language and reviewed them with qualified staff before apprentices repeated difficult work. The notes did not remove every disagreement, but they made the reasons for the next decision easier to explain.

The broader lesson was clear: being able to do a step differs from understanding it. The supervisor kept demonstrations, but also checked whether learners could explain the reasons for safety-critical decisions. Keeping a record of small changes also helped the team distinguish a temporary setback from a lasting problem. For the people involved in an apprentice learns by explaining, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: A shift handover that people could use
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A small care service changed staff at six each evening. Handover notes grew longer, but important details were still missed. The central difficulty was long notes that buried urgent information. Employees copied old descriptions into new forms and had difficulty finding a recent change during a busy handover. A first impression was not enough to tell the whole story, because different people approached the service in different ways.

The group first tried a one-page priority summary. The team placed current actions at the top and kept background records available separately for anyone who needed more detail. The team compared comments with direct observations rather than assuming that the loudest opinion represented everyone.

The trial showed shorter notes supported better questions. Staff could see what had changed, ask for clarification and avoid treating every line as equally urgent. In response, the group adopted a regular review of the summary layout. Supervisors invited workers from day and night shifts to identify information that was still hard to locate. Some suggestions were inexpensive, while others would have required a change to staffing or equipment.

The broader lesson was clear: good handovers make priority visible. The service learned that adding more words is not always the same as communicating more effectively. The final proposal remained open to revision when new information became available. For the people involved in a shift handover that people could use, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: Teaching a new digital form
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A local employer introduced an online leave request form. The instructions described each button, but some employees still submitted incomplete requests. The central difficulty was instructions that assumed prior digital experience. The guide used terms such as attachment and confirmation without showing what they looked like on a phone. Several participants valued the original aim even though they questioned the first method chosen to reach it.

The group first tried a guided demonstration with sample requests. Trainers invited workers to complete a practice form on their own devices and describe where they hesitated. Short conversations after the activity revealed details that a written form had failed to capture.

The trial showed the confirmation step caused most uncertainty. Several people believed a request had been sent when they had only saved a draft. In response, the group adopted screenshots and a visible submission message. The employer added clear images to the guide and changed the final screen to say when a request had been received. The people responsible made their limits clear and invited others to describe any unintended effects.

The broader lesson was clear: teaching should reveal the whole task. A list of buttons was not enough; employees needed to understand the difference between saving and submitting. This approach gave the group a practical basis for its next round of work. For the people involved in teaching a new digital form, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: Mentors exchange their methods
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Experienced workers in a repair centre mentored new colleagues. Each mentor had useful habits, but learners received conflicting advice. The central difficulty was different explanations of the same task. One mentor stressed speed while another emphasised a safety check, leaving apprentices unsure which step was essential. The project began on a small scale so that its organizers could learn before making a permanent commitment.

The group first tried monthly meetings among mentors. Workers compared demonstrations and agreed on the safety steps that everyone should teach, while allowing personal styles elsewhere. They noted both benefits and costs, including the time that volunteers or staff needed to give.

The trial showed a common core reduced confusion. New colleagues could follow one reliable sequence and still learn why experienced staff sometimes chose different optional methods. In response, the group adopted a simple guide with room for examples. Mentors wrote a short shared outline and added notes when a new case showed that an explanation needed improving. The public summary described what had changed and what questions had not yet been answered.

The broader lesson was clear: consistency and experience can support each other. The centre did not demand identical teaching voices; it made essential instructions clear while preserving useful professional judgment. Readers could therefore judge the decision by its evidence rather than by a promise of perfect results. For the people involved in mentors exchange their methods, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A checklist can help a new worker remember the order of a task, but it cannot show whether the worker understands each decision. In a repair workshop, apprentices learned to explain the reason for a step after completing it. When one learner described how to adjust a brake, a short conversation revealed confusion about a damaged cable. A supervisor could correct the misunderstanding before it became a repeated habit. The workshop kept its written instructions and added a notebook of clear explanations. Safety remained the responsibility of qualified staff. The example shows why practical training should include both careful demonstration and opportunities to ask questions about the work.
translation.explanation: 注意whether宾语从句和before引导的时间关系。
translation.referenceAnswer: 检查清单可以帮助新员工记住任务顺序，却不能说明员工是否理解每项决定。在一家维修车间，学徒学会在完成一个步骤后解释其原因。一名学徒说明如何调整刹车时，一段简短对话暴露了他对受损刹车线的误解。主管因此能在误解变成反复出现的习惯前予以纠正。车间保留了书面说明，还增加了一本用清楚语言解释操作的笔记。安全仍由合格员工负责。这个例子说明，实践培训既应包含细致示范，也应提供提问机会。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to a workshop supervisor proposing a way to help adult apprentices understand the reasons behind repair steps. Explain one activity and how the supervisor could assess its value.
writing.explanation: 范文覆盖解释练习、专业安全把关及评估方式。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Supervisor,
I propose adding a brief explanation step after each safe practice repair. An apprentice could tell a partner why a part was checked or replaced, and the partner could ask one question. This would make the reasoning visible without turning every task into a long lesson. A qualified worker should remain responsible for safety decisions and should correct any misunderstanding immediately.
For a month, we could note which steps cause repeated questions and place clear answers in a shared notebook. At the end of the month, supervisors could ask apprentices to explain a new example rather than repeat a memorised list. If they can give the reason for each important action, the activity has helped.
Yours sincerely,
A workshop colleague
